references.text: The beginning of the parable of the prodigal son, where the father has two sons. The older son mentioned in verse 25 is one of these two ([ref:Luk 15:11|Luke 15:11]).

The older son's reaction is further explained: he becomes angry and refuses to go inside, complaining that his father never gave him anything like this, despite his faithful service ([ref:Luk 15:28-30|Luke 15:28-30]).

The context for the entire chapter 15: tax collectors and sinners came near to Jesus, while the Pharisees and scribes murmured. The older son represents the attitude of the Pharisees and scribes toward God accepting sinners ([ref:Luk 15:1-2|Luke 15:1-2]).
The feast that the older son heard music and dancing from was started because the younger son had returned. The father ordered a celebration with the fattened calf ([ref:Luk 15:23-24|Luke 15:23-24]).
The preacher mentions that there is a time to dance – the feast with dancing and music in the parable marks the joy of reunion ([ref:Fork 3:4|Ecclesiastes 3:4]).

David danced for joy when the ark of the covenant was brought to Jerusalem, but Michal, Saul's daughter, despised him – an example that joyful celebration can be met with disapproval from those who watch, just as the older son reacted ([ref:2 Sam 6:14-15|2 Samuel 6:14-15]).

When the Lord brought back the captives of Zion, their mouths were filled with laughter and their tongues with shouts of joy – the joy over reunion and restoration is expressed through celebration and song ([ref:Sal 126:1-2|Psalm 126:1-2]).
Jeremiah's prophecy that Israel will once again adorn themselves and go out in dancing with gladness, a future hope of restoration that reflects the joy in the parable ([ref:Jer 31:4|Jeremiah 31:4]).

The parable of the workers in the vineyard shows a similar attitude: those who worked all day complained that those who came last received the same – the same envious attitude as the older son showed ([ref:Matt 20:11-12|Matthew 20:11-12]).
